title: Given a Scenario, Implement Security Awareness Practices

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Technology alone cannot protect an organization because users make security decisions every day. Security awareness helps users recognize risk, respond correctly, and report suspicious activity to the right people.
The central pattern is to teach users what suspicious behavior looks like, show them how to respond, and reinforce the lesson repeatedly.
sections.callout: Recognition goal: identify the risky behavior in a scenario and the awareness or training practice that best reduces that risk.

entries.title: Phishing
paragraphs: Deceptive communication that attempts to make users reveal information, provide credentials, or take an unsafe action.
entries.recognitionCue: Attacker-controlled deceptive message -> phishing

entries.title: Campaigns
paragraphs: Controlled phishing campaigns use simulated messages to measure and improve awareness. Security teams can identify who recognizes, clicks, or reports the message and where more training is needed.
entries.recognitionCue: Security-controlled simulated phishing for training and measurement -> campaign

entries.title: Recognizing a phishing attempt
paragraphs: Users look for unexpected requests, urgency, suspicious links, unusual attachments, requests for credentials, and impersonation before acting.
entries.recognitionCue: Identify deceptive-message indicators before clicking -> recognize a phishing attempt

entries.title: Responding to reported suspicious messages
paragraphs: Users need a clear reporting process. Once a suspicious message reaches security personnel, they may investigate, block malicious content, search for similar messages, and warn other users.
entries.recognitionCue: A suspicious message reaches security for investigation and action -> reporting response

table.caption: Phishing awareness distinctions
rows: An attacker sends a deceptive message
The organization sends a controlled simulation

entries.title: Anomalous behavior recognition
paragraphs: Identifying human activity that is risky, differs from an expected pattern, or accidentally creates security exposure.
entries.recognitionCue: Notice behavior that may create or reveal security risk -> anomalous behavior recognition

entries.title: Risky behavior
paragraphs: Behavior that increases security exposure, such as sharing credentials, bypassing controls, or using unapproved services.
entries.recognitionCue: The behavior increases the likelihood of a security problem -> risky

entries.title: Unexpected behavior
paragraphs: Behavior that differs from the user's normal pattern, such as suddenly accessing systems unrelated to the person's job.
entries.recognitionCue: The activity deviates from expected behavior -> unexpected

entries.title: Unintentional behavior
paragraphs: An accidental action that creates security exposure, such as sending data to the wrong person, clicking a malicious link, misconfiguring a system, or losing a device.
entries.recognitionCue: No malicious intent, but the action still creates risk -> unintentional

table.caption: Behavior recognition comparison
rows: The action differs from the normal pattern
The action is an accidental mistake

sections.title: User Guidance and Training
paragraphs: Awareness should cover the security situations employees are most likely to encounter and explain how to behave and report concerns.

entries.title: User guidance and training
paragraphs: Instruction and guidance that help personnel recognize risk, respond appropriately, and perform work securely.
entries.recognitionCue: Help users know what to do securely -> guidance and training

entries.title: Policy/handbooks
paragraphs: Written organizational guidance that explains expected behavior, security responsibilities, and reporting requirements.
entries.recognitionCue: Documented employee security expectations -> policy or handbook

entries.title: Situational awareness
paragraphs: Paying attention to current security conditions, including who is nearby, which devices are connected, what information is visible, and whether something seems unusual.
entries.recognitionCue: Understand what is happening in the current environment -> situational awareness

entries.title: Insider threat
paragraphs: Risk from someone with legitimate access who may misuse that access. Training should reinforce recognition and appropriate reporting.
entries.recognitionCue: The risk originates from someone with trusted access -> insider threat

entries.title: Password management
paragraphs: Training should teach users to protect credentials, avoid reuse, use approved password managers, and never share passwords.
entries.recognitionCue: Protect and appropriately manage authentication secrets -> password management

entries.title: Removable media and cables
paragraphs: Unknown USB drives, external storage, charging or data cables, and other removable devices may introduce malware or unauthorized access and should be treated as security risks.
entries.recognitionCue: Unknown removable device or cable -> security risk

entries.title: Social engineering
paragraphs: Manipulation of people into providing information, credentials, access, or money. Common clues include impersonation, urgency, pressure, and unusual requests.
entries.recognitionCue: An attacker manipulates a person -> social engineering

entries.title: Operational security
paragraphs: Protecting sensitive information about systems, schedules, personnel, security processes, and internal operations from unnecessary exposure.
entries.recognitionCue: Protect operational details from disclosure -> operational security

entries.title: Hybrid/remote work environments
paragraphs: Security awareness for work outside normal physical protections, including public Wi-Fi, home networks, device security, screen privacy, and secure remote access.
entries.recognitionCue: Protect users and information outside the traditional office -> hybrid or remote awareness

entries.title: Reporting and monitoring
paragraphs: Measuring awareness results and reinforcing secure behavior over time.
entries.recognitionCue: Collect results and track behavior over time -> reporting and monitoring

entries.title: Initial
paragraphs: The first security-awareness training, provided when a user joins or receives new responsibilities.
entries.recognitionCue: First introduction to security expectations -> initial

entries.title: Recurring
paragraphs: Awareness training that repeats and updates over time because threats change, people forget, and procedures change.
entries.recognitionCue: Ongoing reinforcement and updates -> recurring

entries.title: Development
paragraphs: Designing the awareness program by deciding what users need to learn, which risks to address, which materials to create, and how success will be measured.
entries.recognitionCue: Design and create the awareness program -> development

entries.title: Execution
paragraphs: Delivering and operating the awareness program through training sessions, phishing simulations, communications, and reporting exercises.
entries.recognitionCue: Put the program in front of users -> execution

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Security-controlled simulated email = phishing campaign; attacker-controlled malicious message = phishing
Spot suspicious indicators = recognition; send the message to security = reporting
Behavior increases danger = risky; differs from normal = unexpected; accidental mistake = unintentional
Written employee expectations = policy/handbook; attention to surroundings = situational awareness
Trusted-access risk = insider threat; protect credentials = password management
Unknown USB drive or cable = removable-media risk; manipulate a person = social engineering
Protect operational details = operational security; work securely away from the office = hybrid/remote awareness
First training = initial; ongoing reinforcement = recurring
Build the program = development; deliver the program = execution

sections.title: Objective 5.6 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Awareness helps users recognize security risks, while training teaches them how to respond or perform securely. A controlled phishing simulation is an awareness campaign, not a real attacker-controlled phishing message. When behavior could fit more than one description, use the scenario's emphasis: increased danger, deviation from normal, or accidental action.
sections.callout: The goal is not merely that users took training; the goal is that users recognize risk, behave securely, and report suspicious activity correctly.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Trusted user becomes a risk = insider threat
Unknown USB drive or cable = removable-media risk
Work securely outside the office = hybrid/remote awareness

miniCheck.intro: Classify the training timing and awareness topic.
miniCheck.prompt: Before new employees begin working independently, the organization teaches them not to connect unknown USB drives or data cables to company systems.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. Training delivered before new employees work independently is initial training, and unknown USB drives or data cables are removable-media and cable risks.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Identify whether this is the employees' first security instruction, then identify the device-related risk being taught.
